In contrast, the United States has a relatively low amount of high-speed rail for its size: only 735 kilometers of high-speed rail in operation and 1,789 kilometers under construction. Many US transportation experts argue that this should change, claiming that high-speed rail is more cost-effective than highway systems are.

options: Building successful high-speed rail infrastructure would require that the US government establish a fund to maintain the rail lines long-term.

questions.passage: The roseate spoonbill and the glossy ibis are long-legged birds that live in wetlands, like the Everglades in Florida. Laura D’Acunto and colleagues wanted to know how these birds choose an area in which to live. They looked at features of these birds’ habitats, such as how quickly water drains from the area and the amount of tree-canopy cover there is in the area. They found that roseate spoonbills prefer areas with extensive canopy cover, but this was not true for glossy ibises. The researchers therefore concluded that wetland-management strategies that increase the amount of tree canopy in potential wetland bird habitats are less likely to ______

options: attract glossy ibises to the area than they are to attract roseate spoonbills to the area.
attract birds that don't typically live in wetlands to the area than they are to attract roseate spoonbills or glossy ibises to the area.
decrease the area's appeal to both roseate spoonbills and glossy ibises than they are to increase the appeal to other species.
extend the average lifespan of roseate spoonbills already in the area than they are to attract a greater number of those birds to the area.

questions.passage: The state of Michigan has classified the balsam woolly adelgid as an invasive species that could outcompete some of the state's native species. But researchers Alejandro Camacho and Jason McLachlan have pointed out that Earth's climate is changing in ways that challenge such classifications. Climate changes may cause animals to leave their current ranges and establish new ones. Climate changes may also create good habitats in areas where a species couldn't live previously. These observations suggest that ______

options: Michigan may come to find that categorizing the balsam woolly adelgid as invasive no longer reflects environmental reality.
even if Earth's climate doesn't change in the way scientists predict, the balsam woolly adelgid will likely establish itself in Michigan.
Michigan was previously home to some balsam woolly adelgids but they were outcompeted by invading species.
it's useful at present for Michigan to distinguish between invasive and native species in some instances but not in the case of the balsam woolly adelgid.

One explanation for this is the effort heuristic effect, whereby awareness of the effort invested in a work of art enhances people's appreciation of it. Interestingly, this tendency might also be exploited to mitigate the bias against AI-created art: in another study, participants who had watched videos of robots creating paintings rated the AI-created paintings more favorably than did participants who hadn't watched them, presumably because the videos ______

allayed anxieties about AI replacing human artists.
acknowledged the influence of human-created art on the AI-created paintings.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • From the 1930s to the 1960s, movie theaters in Black communities often created new versions of posters for films to promote Black actors and themes relevant to Black audiences.
  • The original studio poster for Imitation of Life (1934) did not credit any of the film's Black actors.
  • A poster at a Black-owned theater in Harlem, New York, gave top billing to the film's Black star, Louise Beavers, and highlighted the film's theme of Black American identity.
  • According to media historian Ellen Scott, such revisions “centralized African American narrative presence and subjectivity.”
questions.question: The student wants to compare the studio poster for Imitation of Life to the Harlem theater poster. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Harlem theater's poster gave equal billing to all the film's stars—including Beavers—while highlighting themes of Black American identity.
Compared to the Harlem theater poster, the studio poster gave far less attention to Beavers, listing her name but not identifying her as one of the film's stars.
While the studio poster did not even name the film's Black actors, the Harlem poster promoted both Beavers and the film's theme of Black American identity.
The Harlem theater poster promoted the film's Black star and the film's relevance to Black audiences; thus, it “centralized African American narrative presence and subjectivity.”

Though Leptecophylla tameiameiae and Schinus terebinthifolia can both be found in Oahu, Hawaii, only the former plant is native.

  • In a 2020 article, art historian Ariel Bonilla analyzed Smith's response to the Columbus quincentennial celebration.

  • Bonilla: Smith's show was “disinterested in financial gain as a primary or even secondary motivation.”
questions.question: The student wants to use a quotation from Bonilla to explain Smith's motivation for curating the show. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: According to Bonilla, Smith curated The Submuloc Show/Columbus Wohs as “a visual commentary on the Columbus quincentennial from the perspective of America’s first people.”

According to Bonilla, Smith was “disinterested in financial gain as a primary or even secondary motivation” in her curation of the exhibition, a celebration of the 500th anniversary of Columbus's first voyage to the Americas.
According to Bonilla, Smith's “primary or even secondary motivation” for curating the show was to analyze Columbus from the perspective of a Native artist.
According to Bonilla, Smith curated the exhibition to “create a counter-narrative” in response to the Columbus quincentennial, one focused instead on “Native American survival.”

questions.passage: Can artificial intelligence (AI) truly capture human consciousness? Louisa Hall's novel Speak pursues this inquiry by weaving together five stories across different centuries, from a Puritan woman's diary to an AI's confessions. These narratives reveal unexpected connections, suggesting that our drive to preserve human expression through technology stems from fear that without such mediation, our voices might be lost to time. Hall ultimately posits that AI represents not merely a technological achievement but the latest manifestation of an existential attempt to transcend mortality.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a provocative paradox, summarizes how a novel questions the assumptions underlying the paradox, and reframes the author's message as an argument about AI and human mortality.

It poses a philosophical dilemma, outlines five storylines that explore this dilemma across different time periods, and reveals how these stories converge to challenge conventional views about technology.

It begins with a question about the role of AI in society, explains how an author seeks to answer that question in a novel, and proposes that preserving human expression is more important than technological advancement.

It introduces a novel's central question, describes how the author employs a specific narrative structure to investigate that question, and presents the author's conclusion about a broader human concern.

questions.passage: Most Native languages belong to language families, or groups of languages whose structural and lexical correspondence likely derives from their descent from a single language spoken long ago. A minority—such as Kootenai, which is spoken in Idaho and Montana, and Tunica, which is spoken in Louisiana—are isolates, having no demonstrable genealogical relationship to other languages. Yet Kootenai and Tunica, like all isolates, are potentially remnants of families whose other members vanished before the historical record could attest to them, perhaps through the geographical expansion of extant families.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It proposes that the distinction made between present-day nonisolate languages and isolates like Kootenai and Tunica may not have been applicable in the distant past.
It asserts that the historical record tends to overrepresent nonisolate languages relative to isolates, such that the origins of Kootenai and Tunica are obscure to scholars in the present day.
It suggests that the ancestral languages of both Kootenai and Tunica were likely isolates that replaced nonisolate languages through geographic expansion in the distant past.
It implies that a nonisolate language may have influenced both Kootenai and Tunica to such a degree that their relationship to their former families is no longer discernible.
